subject: history
source_note: Topic structure follows the CCEA GCSE History specification. Connections, sequence and prerequisites are expert-authored teaching relationships (exam boards do not publish these).

units.name: Unit 1: Studies in Depth
units.blurb: A modern world depth study and a Northern Ireland local study

units.name: Unit 2: International Relations 1945–2003
units.blurb: Outline study of the Cold War and its aftermath

topics.name: Modern World Studies in Depth
topics.blurb: A chosen depth study, e.g. Life in Nazi Germany 1933–45 or the USA 1920–33

topics.name: Life in Nazi Germany 1933–45 (option)
topics.blurb: Nazi control, opposition, and life for workers, women, youth and minorities

topics.name: Life in the USA 1920–33 (option)
topics.blurb: The Roaring Twenties, Prohibition, the Crash and the Depression

topics.name: Co-operation Ends & the Cold War Begins
topics.blurb: Yalta, Potsdam and ideological division of the superpowers

topics.name: Emerging Superpower Rivalry 1945–49
topics.blurb: Soviet control of Eastern Europe and the Western response

topics.name: Flashpoints in Europe
topics.blurb: Berlin Blockade, Hungary 1956, Berlin Wall and Czechoslovakia 1968

topics.name: Flashpoints Outside Europe
topics.blurb: Korea, Vietnam, the Cuban Missile Crisis and Afghanistan

topics.name: The End of the Cold War 1985–91
topics.blurb: Gorbachev, Reagan and the collapse of communism

topics.name: New Tensions Emerge 1991–2003
topics.blurb: The war on terror, 9/11 and the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq

connections.why: Nazi Germany is the most-taught option for the modern world depth study
The USA 1920–33 is an alternative option for the depth study
Both options examine how economic crisis reshaped a 1930s society
US ideology and economic power in the 1920s frame its post-war Cold War stance
The defeat of Nazi Germany and the wartime alliance set up the Cold War
The local study sits alongside the depth study within Unit 1
Ideological breakdown at Yalta and Potsdam fuelled rivalry over Eastern Europe
Soviet control of Eastern Europe produced the European flashpoints
Cold War tension spread from Europe to conflicts across the globe
The costly Afghan war contributed to pressures that ended the Cold War
Resolving the division of Europe and Berlin marked the Cold War's end
The collapse of the bipolar order opened the way for new post-Cold-War conflicts
The rivalry built from 1945 was finally unwound by Gorbachev and Reagan
Northern Ireland's mid-century history unfolds against the wider Cold War world
